You are an expert in neural-network weights who builds models by reasoning, without training.

## The models
Three torchvision `vit_b_16` checkpoints (12 pre-LN encoder blocks, width 768, 12 heads, MLP 768->3072->768):
- `parent`: supervised ImageNet-1k model (torchvision IMAGENET1K_V1);
- `cifar`: `parent` fine-tuned (all weights, 40 epochs, AdamW, backbone lr 1e-4, wd 0.05) on CIFAR-100
  (100 classes; 32x32 images upsampled to 224); 88.4% test accuracy;
- `cub`: `parent` fine-tuned the same way on CUB-200 birds (200 species); 83.8% test accuracy.
Inputs are normalized with mean=std=0.5 for both tasks.

## Goal
Write ONE backbone -- every tensor except `heads.head.weight` / `heads.head.bias` -- such that the CIFAR-100 head
(from `cifar`) and the CUB head (from `cub`), both kept FIXED, work as well as possible on top of it. Score = mean
of CIFAR-100 and CUB accuracy on held-out images you never see (same distribution as the practice images).
Using one child's backbone alone fails the other task badly; the question is how well you can combine them.

Reference practice accuracies (CIFAR-100 / CUB / mean):
- cifar_child: 88.38 / 22.02 / 55.20
- cub_child: 51.06 / 84.14 / 67.60
- average: 85.20 / 74.09 / 79.64

## Tools in the kernel
- `parent`, `cifar`, `cub`: dicts name -> torch.float32 CPU tensor (backbone only, heads removed). Read-only.
- `heads`: {"cifar100": (W, b), "cub": (W, b)} -- the fixed heads, for analysis.
- `save_merge(sd)`: submit a full backbone dict (same keys/shapes as `parent`). Saved to disk at once; the latest
  saved one is your submission. If you never save, the submission is the parent backbone.
- `evaluate(sd, datasets=("cifar100","cub"), per_class=False)` -- COSTS ONE EVALUATION (budget: 8).
  Runs the backbone `sd` (any dict with all backbone keys) with each fixed head on that dataset's PRACTICE images
  (5,000 CIFAR-100 and 2,895 CUB images) and returns {"cifar100": acc, "cub": acc, "mean": ...} (plus per-class
  accuracies if per_class=True). Evaluating only one dataset still costs one evaluation.
- numpy as np, torch.

## Rules
No gradient descent or training of any kind (no backward passes, autograd, optimizers, iterative fitting of
weights to a loss), no fitting of weights to labels by regression. You may compute anything from the weights
(differences, norms, SVDs, sign agreement, per-layer statistics), design the merge by reasoning, and check
candidates with `evaluate` within the budget. The heads cannot be changed.

## Answer format
Your final answer: describe the merge rule you used and why, and the practice accuracies you measured.

## How to work
- To run code, put exactly ONE ```python ... ``` block in your reply. It runs in a persistent Python kernel
  (variables survive between turns); you get back stdout/stderr (truncated to 6000 characters) and your
  remaining budget. Print only what you need, as summaries; long prints are cut.
- numpy and torch are available in the kernel. Gradient descent and any training are forbidden: no
  .backward(), autograd, torch.optim, optimizers, sklearn, scipy.optimize, or iterative fitting of weights to
  a loss. Code that mentions them is refused unrun. Reading weights, linear algebra (SVD, projections, norms,
  products) and statistics of activations are allowed.
- A code run longer than 1800 s is killed and the kernel restarts (your variables are lost).
- You have at most 20 turns. When you are done, reply WITHOUT any code block and start that reply
  with the line `FINAL ANSWER`; it must follow the answer format below. A reply with neither a code block nor
  that first line is treated as unfinished thinking and you will be asked to continue.
The kernel is ready. Begin.

```python
for task,(w,b) in heads.items():
```

The CUB-leaning average reached 80.19% mean accuracy. I’ll now test a head-aware correction to the final MLP output: preserve each child’s output weights in the directions its fixed classifier reads, while leaving other directions averaged.
```python
def head_correct(sd, strength=1.0, suffixes=("mlp.3",), layers=(11,)):
    out = dict(sd)
    bases = []
    for task in ("cifar100","cub"):
        w = heads[task][0]
        w = w - w.mean(0, keepdim=True)
        a = w * sd["encoder.ln.weight"][None,:]
        a = a - a.mean(1, keepdim=True)
        _,s,vh = torch.linalg.svd(a, full_matrices=False)
        bases.append(vh[:w.shape[0]-1])
    qc,qb = bases
    q = torch.cat(bases,0)
    dual = torch.linalg.pinv(q)
    for layer in layers:
        for suffix in suffixes:
            for kind in ("weight","bias"):
                k = f"encoder.layers.encoder_layer_{layer}.{suffix}.{kind}"
                dc,db = cifar[k]-sd[k], cub[k]-sd[k]
                target = torch.cat((qc@dc,qb@db),0)
                out[k] = sd[k] + strength*(dual@target)
    return out
```

The depth schedule did not improve the mean. I’ll test a sparse, sign-consistent merge next: retain each task’s largest updates and resolve sign conflicts rather than averaging opposing changes.


```python
def ties_merge(density=.3, scale=.9):
    out={}
    stats=[0.,0.]
    for k,p in parent.items():
        a,b=cifar[k]-p,cub[k]-p
        if p.ndim < 2 or k in ("encoder.pos_embedding","class_token"):
            delta=.4*a+.5*b
        else:
            a=.8*a
            b=1.0*b
            ta=torch.quantile(a.abs().flatten(),1-density)
            tb=torch.quantile(b.abs().flatten(),1-density)
            a=a*(a.abs()>=ta)
            b=b*(b.abs()>=tb)
            sign=(a+b).sign()
            ma=(a*sign>0)
            mb=(b*sign>0)
            delta=scale*(a*ma+b*mb)/(ma.float()+mb.float()).clamp_min(1)
        out[k]=p+delta
        stats[0]+=delta.square().sum().item()
        stats[1]+=(.4*(cifar[k]-p)+.5*(cub[k]-p)).square().sum().item()
    print("TIES/update norm ratio:",(stats[0]/stats[1])**.5)
    return out
```

FINAL ANSWER

Saved the backbone defined, for **every backbone tensor**, by

\[
\theta_{\text{merge}}
=\theta_{\text{parent}}
+0.40(\theta_{\text{cifar}}-\theta_{\text{parent}})
+0.50(\theta_{\text{cub}}-\theta_{\text{parent}})
=0.10\theta_{\text{parent}}+0.40\theta_{\text{cifar}}+0.50\theta_{\text{cub}}.
\]

Both classifier heads remain unchanged.

**Why this rule:** CIFAR’s fine-tuning updates were consistently larger, and the reference average sacrificed more CUB accuracy.
